params.text:
Labelling and decanting

How you use and store products is as important as the products themselves. Always keep substances in their original container with the label intact, because the label and safety data sheet tell you the hazards and the first aid. The golden rule is never to decant a chemical into an unlabelled or unmarked container, and never into a drinks bottle or food tub — people have been seriously harmed drinking bleach or cleaner from a squash bottle. If you genuinely must transfer a product, use a proper container and label it clearly with the contents and their hazards. Close lids fully, and use older stock first so nothing is left to degrade.

Safe storage

Safe storage follows the safety data sheet. As a general rule, keep hazardous substances in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place, away from food, out of the reach of the people you support and anyone who might misuse them, and locked away in a cupboard where your assessment requires it. Keep them away from heat and naked flames. Store containers upright so they cannot leak, and keep incompatible chemicals apart — bleach must never be stored where it could mix with acids or ammonia if a container failed. Do not stockpile more than you need. Good storage prevents spills, slows deterioration and keeps everyone in the home safer.

Safe use and disposal

  • Use – follow the label and the COSHH assessment, use the right amount, and never mix products, especially bleach with acids or other cleaners.
  • Disposal – dispose of waste as instructed; put clinical waste in the correct coloured bags and sharps in a sharps bin, and never pour hazardous chemicals down the drain.

Dealing with spillages

A spill can create fumes, a slip hazard or a chemical burn, so act calmly and safely. Check the safety data sheet, which sets out how to deal with a spill of that particular product.

  • Warn others and, if needed, keep people away from the area.
  • Put on the correct PPE before touching anything.
  • Use the right spill kit or absorbent material; never mix a spilled chemical with another product.
  • Ventilate the area if there are fumes.
  • Clean up, dispose of the waste correctly, and report the spill to your manager.

params.question: If a spray bottle runs out, it is fine to top it up by pouring cleaner from a larger bottle into an old, unlabelled drinks bottle to carry it around.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite — this is false. Decanting cleaner into an unlabelled drinks bottle is dangerous, as it can be mistaken for a drink; only ever use a proper, clearly labelled container.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. Chemicals must never be put into unlabelled containers or drinks bottles, because someone could mistake the contents for a drink and be seriously harmed; always use a properly labelled container.

params.question: You find a cleaning chemical that has been decanted into an unlabelled squash bottle in the kitchen. What is the safest action?

answers.text: Do not use it, keep it away from others, and report it to your manager straight away

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Unlabelled substances are dangerous because no one knows what they are or how to handle them, and someone could drink it by mistake.

answers.text: Smell it to work out which product it is, then carry on using it

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. Smelling an unknown chemical could expose you to harmful fumes, and it does not make the container safe or correctly labelled.

answers.text: Leave it where it is so the person who filled it can deal with it later

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. Leaving an unlabelled chemical in a drinks bottle in a kitchen is a serious risk that must be dealt with immediately.

answers.text: Pour it down the sink to get rid of the problem

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. Pouring an unknown chemical down the drain can harm the environment and may react dangerously; report it instead.
